utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor against Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Thursday. I would first of all like to greet the accused, Defence counsel, all the members of the OTP, as well as all the people assisting us. I would, first of all, like to read out an oral decision handed down by the Chamber. Oral decision regarding time allocation in light of Milivoj Petkovic's testimony. On the 28th of January, 2010, the Praljak Defence asked to have two hours overall to cross-examine Milivoj Petkovic. In addition, the Stojic Defence and the Coric Defence have both asked the Chamber, in two applications filed on the 5th and 9th of February, 2010, respectively, to have an extra hour, in addition to the time that would be allocated to them by the Trial Chamber, pursuant to Practice Direction number 5 of the decision of the 24th of April, 2008, to cross-examine Milivoj Petkovic. The Petkovic Defence indicated that it did not object to the Praljak Defence application, nor to the Stojic Defence application, and two replies filed on 5th and 8th of February, 2010, respectively.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "Not practice direction," but "guide-lines," please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On 9th of February, 2010, the Prosecution also filed a reply to the Praljak and Stojic Defence applications, in which it asked the Trial Chamber, first of all, to amend its practices as regarded time allocation at the hearing when the Defence witnesses were to testify. It objects, and that is the second point to the Praljak Defence and Stojic Defence applications. And, lastly, if the Trial Chamber were to grant these two applications, it would ask the Trial Chamber to grant it extra time to cross-examine Milivoj Petkovic, i.e., 50 per cent of their overall time that has been accorded to the Defence teams for their cross-examination. On the 10th of February, 2010, the Petkovic Defence indicated that it objected to the extra time application of the Prosecution, as well as an amendment of the guide-lines as far as time allocation was concerned during the cross-examination of Defence witnesses. The Trial Chamber notes that all the other parties have not filed a response to the applications filed by Praljak and Stojic Defences and the Prosecution. In addition, due to the fact that the application was filed rather late by the Coric Defence, the Trial Chamber feels that it is not necessary to wait for the answers, if any, by the parties regarding this application. After having looked into the positions of the various parties, the Trial Chamber notes that in light of the 65 ter summary of the testimony of the accused Petkovic, nothing justifies extra time to be allocated to the parties, pursuant to the decision of 24th of April, 2008, to conduct their respective cross-examinations. Consequently, the Trial Chamber decides to dismiss the applications filed by the Stojic Defence, the Praljak Defence, the Coric Defence, and the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber, therefore, decides to allocate the time in the courtroom as follows: The Petkovic Defence will have six hours to conduct its examination-in-chief of Milivoj Petkovic. The Prosecution will have six hours to conduct its cross-examination. The Prlic Defence and Stojic Defence teams, Praljak, Coric, and Pusic Defence teams, will have, all in all, three hours, i.e., 36 minutes each to be shared between them. The Trial Chamber recalls, however, that the Defence teams can agree between them on how these three hours need to be allocated, and invites them, thereby, to inform the Trial Chamber of the way they wish to proceed, if necessary. Registrar, you have a few numbers to give us, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness 4D-AA. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit IC01170. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit IC01171. And the list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit IC01172. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition, the Trial Chamber has been seized, on the 10th of February, 2010, of an application to add on the 65 ter list documents which are in the annex. The Trial Chamber is, therefore, asking the parties, Prosecution and Defence teams, to let us know today what their positions are on this application to add 16 documents. I think, Ms. Alaburic, that you had something to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I have to say that I have nothing to inform you about. I'd just like to thank you for your decision, and I am pleased to see that we're going to start with the examination today. But I think Mr. Scott wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and thank you, Counsel. Good morning to Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Your Honour, I can give the Chamber the Prosecution's position on the additional exhibits now, and I'm happy to say, perhaps especially in light of some of the exchange in the written pleadings that were filed on the other issue, the Prosecution has no objection to those. And as far as the Prosecution is concerned, they can be added. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall, therefore, bring General Petkovic into the courtroom [as interpreted] -- bring him to the witness stand. General, I hope your microphone is working. For the transcript, I would like to greet you once again. I would like you to give us your first name, last name, and date of birth, please. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. I'm Milivoj Petkovic. I was born on the 11th of October, 1949, in Sibenik, the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Like I proceed with other witnesses, I would like to know from you what your occupation was. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at present I'm retired. Otherwise, I spent my whole working life as an army man, and the last post was the chief inspector in the Army of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. General, have you testified before a court of law on the events that unfolded in the former Yugoslavia? And if that is the case, which court did you testify before and in what case? THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I testified before this Tribunal in two cases, the first being the Blaskic trial, and the second was the Kordic and Cerkez trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Blaskic case, were you a Prosecution witness, a Defence witness, or a witness of the Court? THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in both cases I was a Court witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you to read the solemn declaration. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, what I'm going to tell you is going to be short, since it is only the third time that you are taking the stand, so you know full well how all of this takes place. Moreover, you have attended the proceedings in this courtroom for a number of years now, so there is nothing new for you. You will have to answer the questions put to you by your counsel, Ms. Alaburic. After that, I believe I will put some questions to you. Other Defence counsel will then put questions to you, and then the Prosecutor, Mr. Prosecutor, I believe in this case, will cross-examine you. Ms. Alaburic will undoubtedly take the floor again for her redirect. This, all in all, should take a few weeks. This is what I wanted to share with you, and I would like to welcome you once again. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, once again. And, once again, good morning to you. Once again, good morning to you all. Good morning to the Prosecution, and particularly Mr. Scott. Good morning to everybody on the Defence and everybody else who is with us today. I would like to inform you at this point that the Defence of General Petkovic, or, rather, my colleague Mr. Nicholas Stewart and myself, will not be having any contacts with our client during his testimony, not even during the examination-in-chief, and our communication with General Petkovic will be reduced to technical matters, if he needs a document or any other technical assistance. And in all such -- if I do have any such communication, I shall inform the Trial Chamber so that you know exactly what our contacts with the general have been, if any.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's start off with some information that is pertinent from your curriculum vitae. You know the procedure. I'm going to read that out, and you're either going to confirm them, if they are correct, or say so if they're not. You said, General, that you were born on the 11th of October in 1949, and you were born in Sibenik in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as your education is concerned, I think it's important for the Trial Chamber to hear that you have -- you graduated from the Pedagogical Gymnasium and then the Military Academy for the Land Army in Belgrade. And in Belgrade, you studied from 1968 to 1972. You completed specialist training for missile and anti-armoured units in 1976. Next, in 1979 you graduated from a training course for military personnel at a military school in Sarajevo. You graduated in 1983 from the Command Staff School of the JNA. And in the Republic of Croatia, you took part in three workshops on the work of NATO command and staff, and those workshops were organised by retired officers of the United States Army. General, is the information I've presented correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The following information is important for your career.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we've heard a witness whose name I won't mention, because he was a protected witness. He told us that he also underwent training with American generals. When he told me that, I thought that it might be training initiated by the United States of America as part of co-operation with Croatia, or was it some private organisation that had had former US officers to "sell," quote/unquote, a training course to all those people who wanted to attend this course? This course you had in these three workshops, this was part of what? Why was it organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was organised at the level of the two defence ministries, the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and the Ministry of Defence of the United States of America. The school, made up of retired officers - in this case it was General Vuono who headed it - offered its service all over the world. But the contract wasn't made with the school directly but with the ministry of each individual country, so that General Vuono and his team worked in the Republic of Croatia for many years, starting with the Guards Army and the units there, and the other was with superior commands -- or, rather, the superior commands worked with the superior levels of command and control, from brigadiers onwards, regardless of whether they were commanders of brigades or whether they were in the staff of the operative zone or in the Main Staff. That's how the groups were formed. And this same group - let me just finish - for Bosnia-Herzegovina, this same group led by General Vuono, according to the programme, it was called "Equip and Train," and after the Dayton Agreement it provided services to officers in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or now rather the Army of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to finish off with this question, can you tell me on what date you started this training course as part of the signature of an agreement between Croatia and the United States of America? When did you start your training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the training course in the Republic of Croatia started -- I think it was in 1976. I'm sorry, I said "1976." I meant 1996. That was when it started, with the lower structures, that is to say, the units, and then the following year it was continued at the command levels, according to a Ministry of Defence plan, and the plan was adopted by the group. And I became part of it in 1996. And since there were several subjects that were offered - you could choose between several subjects - I chose three relating to the staff command and NATO structures and so on and so forth, and that went on for seven or, rather, ten days. Perhaps General Praljak can put the date right. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I don't want to say anything leading, but I think that General Petkovic has said "1996" twice, so I'd like him to think again about when the general started working in Croatia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I started in 1996. They started in 1994. So 1994 was the beginning, and various structures were operating, and I became part of that in 1996, in the latter part. There were others after me, but I thought it was sufficient to complete that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I asked you a question about the date, it was because it was important, if I asked you a question about the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation hadn't been completed, and, General Petkovic, you are speaking extremely fast. Could you slow down, please? The interpreters would be very grateful if you would slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, please slow down. What I wanted to say is this: If I put this question about the date, it is because it is important. And I am discovering that this training started in 1994. You attended in 1996, but the training course was actually organised in 1994. Was this training organised in 1994, when the conflict still existed between the HVO and the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in 1994 I did not attend that training course. On the 5th of August, 1994, I left the HVO, and the first time I attended the course was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question. I'm not going to dwell on this. Maybe you are unable to answer the question. If that's the case, please let us know. When you started your course in 1996, which was an official course since it was part of an agreement between two governments, as far as you know, did the US government select the Croatian people going on the course or did they accept all those people who signed up for the training course, without the Americans selecting anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the choice was made by the representatives of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and a part of us who had completed the JNA schools joined up only at the end. They said we didn't need the first part, the part of the course which was taught at lower levels. So the Republic of Croatia -- rather, the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff, based on the development plan for the Personnel Department and each individual officer, they selected the people to attend those courses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, now a few words about your career. You became employed in the Yugoslav People's Army, and you were in Slovenia. You served in Slovenia from 1972 until 1979. Then you transferred to Zadar, and you were at the Military Academy there from 1979 to 1991, and you worked there dealing with the training of artillery cadres. Your last rank in the Yugoslav People's Army was a lieutenant-colonel. You left the JNA in July 1991, and on the 1st of August, 1991, on the basis of a decision terminating your service, the status of officer of the JNA was equally terminated officially. You next joined the Croatian Army, and you co-operated with the Croatian Army since the 26th of July as a volunteer. Yes, July. And we said on the 1st of August, 1991, you officially left the JNA, and you officially became a commander for the defence of Sibenik, first of all, on the basis of a contract with the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, and from the 1st of December, 1991 -- or, rather, November 1991, with the Republic of Croatia Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the date, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of November, 1991, you were deployed to the Command of the Split Operative Zone in the Operations Department or for Operational Affairs. And on the 14th of April, 1992, you were deployed to Grude, to Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the Forward Command Post of the Southern Front, as deputy commander to Janko Bobetko. And from that time onwards, on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you spent until the 24th of July, 1993, as chief of the Main Staff of the HVO. And after that period, until the 9th of November, 1993, you were deputy commander of the Main Staff of the HVO, that is to say, General Praljak. And after that, from the 9th of November, 1993, until the 26th of April, 1994, you were deputy chief of the HVO Main Staff, Ante Roso. And from the 26th of April, 1994, to the 5th of August, 1994, you were chief of the Main Staff of the HVO. At that time, you left Bosnia-Herzegovina to return to the Croatian Army. And from the 1st of November, 1994, you were deployed as chief of staff of the Military District of Osijek. And six months later, you were transferred as deputy commander of the Osijek Military District. After that, from the 23rd of March, 1996, to the 3rd of January, 2003, you were commander of the Military District of Ston, with its headquarters in Dubrovnik. And from the 1st of January, 2003 -- or the 3rd of January, 2003, until April of that same year, you were the chief inspector of defence of the Republic of Croatia. You retired in July 2004 as colonel of the Croatian Army. That was your last rank. Is that information correct, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Perhaps I could make a correction. I officially left the JNA on the 1st of August. That's when I received my papers from the JNA. The fact that I left several days before was their goodwill to allow me to leave the barracks. They said, Leave the barracks and you can wait for your papers to arrive. So although I was still in the JNA for a few days, I wasn't actually working, and that was a sort of gift from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just correct the transcript, because the last rank you held in the army was colonel-general of the Croatian Army. Yes, that's fine now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General - you have corrected me - when we discussed your CV, you mentioned that you left the JNA based on an official decision. What was the reason for your insistence on the paperwork to be done in accordance with the rules?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had the right to leave the JNA after eight years of service because my contract that I signed with them only stipulated that I stay twice the length of my military training or education, and that only lasted four years. So after eight years, I could have applied to be discharged, but I held out until 1991. That was the year when Slovenia and Croatia were announcing their departure from Yugoslavia. Croatia was already facing a three months' moratorium. The Artillery Training Centre in which I served, on the 22nd of June started relocating some of its elements outside the Zadar Garrison for reasons of security, as they said. And then the School of Reserve Officers, to which I returned, for security reasons was relocated to the Benkovac Garrison, which was the center of the rebellion in Croatia. You can imagine, in Zadar, a predominantly Croatian city, the army feels unsafe and moves to Benkovac. Other elements of the Training Centre were preparing to relocate to Sarajevo. That was the first option, and if that would prove unfeasible, Belgrade was the second option. It became clear to me that, in practice, there were no real negotiations about the reorganisation of Croatia. Being a Croat and born in Croatia, where all my relatives are, it was unimaginable to me to leave Croatia to go with the JNA to Macedonia, or any other place, to continue living there and make a living that way as then already things started happening that shocked the Croatian public, such as the events at Plitvice, where allegedly rebel Serbs who actually came out of JNA APCs attacked the police force of Croatia, and then Borovo Selo. Behind all these incidents, there was the JNA, because it is obvious from the footage made that these weren't Serb volunteers or rebel Serbs, but rather the JNA. So in Zadar, we raised the question why the railroad lines out of Benkovac, Knin, Gracac, Zagreb was blocked and why the army did not unblock that important railroad line in Croatia. The reply we received was that it wasn't for us to worry about that, that there was a general staff, the so-called SSNO, who was monitoring the situation and would take adequate steps. In the meantime --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I just want to ask you to cut short this part because we'll run out of time.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So, basically, the JNA in the Zadar Garrison was planned to leave Zadar and move out of Croatia, and that didn't suit me. I was born neither in Serbia, nor in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and without Croatia there could be no Yugoslavia in which I wanted to live. I didn't want to run away, which some people had done, and there was a recommendation by the federal secretary for everybody to leave who felt like that, and that's what I did. I was even escorted by my commander to the gate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, until that time, until the late 1980s, were you satisfied with your life and work in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, I certainly was. The salary wasn't high, but the salaries were still higher than those paid out in the private or social-owned economy. My wife -- or, rather, I even was allotted an apartment within three months. Others had to wait for years. My career advanced rapidly. So I was, all in all, satisfied, but the time came when I had to leave the JNA, which became what it became at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You told us, General, that in 2003 you were appointed chief inspector of defence of the Republic of Croatia. Tell us, was that a promotion or not? Was it an advancement in your military career or something else?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to everything I had gone through in Croatia until that time, it was an advancement in my career. Having said that, I would like to add that I left the HVO as chief of main staff of an army, that was my title, and I returned to the Croatian Army, to zone of operations, as a third man there, because they said to me, Well, you'll be given the post of operations officer, and your next post will be that of a staff officer. Take it or leave it. I accepted. And where I had left off in the Croatian Army, that's the same level at which I started again after this interval.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who was the minister of defence at that time, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Gojko Susak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: It was Ms. -- I'm stalled.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Zeljka Antunovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Zeljka Antunovic, a member of the SDP. Before her, it was Mr. Rados, who was also from the coalition government.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: "SDP" stands for the Social Democratic Party; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, who was president of Croatia at that time in 2003?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stipe Mesic. He still has a few days left and then he'll be leaving.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, do you consider yourself a professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I most certainly do, because I have everything it takes to be a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us your personal view, General. Does the quality of work of -- or can the quality of work of a professional soldier depend on the programme of the ruling party? Or, in other words, you will be a good soldier/officer if the Christian democrats are in power, but you will be less good if the social democrats are in power? What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the quality of your work only depends on what you know and how you go about your work. Another issue is whether the party that is in power at the time appreciates it appropriately. There were instances of people being selected by computer to retire because there was a down-sizing process in place in Croatia that included officers, NCOs, and soldiers. I must add that the political suitability also played a role in that respect, and that is how the computer recognised them. And when I say "computer," that's, of course, a metaphor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Speaking from the point of view of a professional soldier, should he go about his job regardless of who is in power or will he behave differently depending on that element?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: There can be no difference. We all know what it means to be a professional, and in your working hours you must go about your job professionally, irrespective of who is in power. Another issue is how that will be appreciated, because the criteria can be different, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, what's your opinion? Should the objectives of an army be set by the civilian authorities or can the army, itself, define the reasons of its existence and the objectives of its actions?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is clear that these objectives are set by politics rather than the military. The military must implement these decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, regarding where you were positioned, I have two questions to ask you. The first one is the following: When you were within the JNA, were you a member of the Yugoslav Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I joined the League of Communists during the second year of military academy. And to be honest, when I left the JNA I forgot to leave the League of Communists, but probably when I left the army I probably automatically ceased to be a member of that organisation. But throughout my army career, except for the two years at the beginning of my training, I was a member of the League of Communists; that is, 21 years in all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you were a member of the League of Communists, was it because it matched your ideals, or did you have to become a member if you wanted to reach higher ranks? In other words, was it not possible to reach higher ranks if you were not a member of the League of Communists, so did you join for that reason, or did you join because of ideological reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me explain. When you are admitted to a military academy, they start monitoring you, they say, You're studying well, and so on, and the party is present in your platoon, your company, in your generation. It's there. You cannot do anything without the party being involved. Once you complete a training that lasts for a month, it is normal to analyse that training subsequently, and the military structures take part in that, but there's also the party that has its say and points out how party members fared in that training and how they influenced others, who were not party members, to go about their duties and responsibilities. So you couldn't make a single move in your unit without the party being present. So sometimes there were the three levels talking about the same thing; the military collective, then the command structure of that collective, and the party, and there was a fourth. That was the Union of Socialist Youth. It was also present in the military and military schools. So there were two political structures that also had its say about all of us. For example, toward the end of my first year in military school, the party also assessed my performance, what I could have done better, or worse, or whatever. So the party was present everywhere, and what -- and I want to say something else, too. It was essential to your career to be a party member, so people considered that -- well, that party sanctions are a more serious impediment to your advancement than disciplinary punishment. If you were thrown out of the party, you could remain in the JNA, but you wouldn't be promoted for 50 years, and they would find you a position somewhere out of the way. So the party basically determined your development and your advancement. You couldn't become a division commander without being a member of the League of Communists, or even battalion commander. You could be company command, because they would think, Well, he's still young, he still has time to join the party. But at the meetings of that organisation, they would try to induce you to join.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a second question to put to you. When you left the HVO, you said that you went back to the Croatian Army, and you were the third man or number three in an operative zone. And I believe I understood, but perhaps I'm wrong. Through what you said, I had the feeling that, in a way, you were rather disappointed. Perhaps you found that given that you had a very high rank within the HVO, you could have expected to have a similar rank or position, whereas, in fact, you were only number three. And you also specified that at the time, the minister of defence was Mr. Susak. Could you perhaps tell me if this appointment did not take into account the role you had within the HVO? Given that you were a volunteer within the HVO, the Croatian Army, did it have to take this on board? Was that some sort of a sanction, or was there any other reason for this appointment? Could you perhaps tell us what is your personal opinion as to why you were appointed at that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wouldn't say that it was any sort of punishment or me being ignored. At that time, Croatia had a lot of its own commanders and generals who had been in war in Croatia all that time, so it would not have been appropriate, irrespective of the fact that I'd been the chief of the Main Staff there, to have people removed because of me. I was very glad that neither the minister of defence nor the chief of staff made such moves, although I had been promised that I would be in charge of military education. That was one of the options. But there was a person there who had two years until retirement, after having worked there for three or four years, and they didn't want to eliminate them, and that was okay. I accepted the post of the chief of staff in the Military District Osijek because I'd been told how the professional developments would go there. My first deputy soon joined the Office of the President of the Republic, and there were also announcements that the commander would also leave and join the Ministry of Defence. So within a very short period of time, I would become the commander of the military region. However, it didn't happen that way. The commander stayed on a bit longer, and in the meantime the Croatian Army was reorganised and a new military district was set up in the south of Croatia under number 4, Military District 4, and what was offered to me was either to wait for the commander in Osijek to be reassigned and then for me to take his position, or I was offered to go to Dubrovnik. Being a Dalmatian, I accepted to go to Dubrovnik, and in Dubrovnik I established a military district. And then after seven years, due to a new reorganisation of the Croatian Army, I closed the military district. And I hold the record in those terms, because I was a military district commander for seven years. I didn't object to being the commander of that district, because Dubrovnik is a wonderful place. I don't like big towns like Zagreb. I had peace and quiet over there. And at the end of the day, when I was offered that position -- or, rather, when I was offered to become the inspector of defence, I had two or three more years before retirement, and that's why I accepted that position. And I remained in the position until I was transferred to Scheveningen, to the Detention Unit, and here I don't hold any function or positions, as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Alaburic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, what is your position? In a well-organised society, do civilian authorities exert control over the military?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The civilian authorities do control the military. I -- as the chief inspector of defence in the Republic of Croatia, I was not subordinated to the supreme commander. I was subordinated to the minister of defence, and the minister of defence is a member of the Government of the Republic of Croatia, i.e., a member of the civilian authorities, which means I was not subordinated to the supreme commander and I didn't fall under the category of those who were members of the armed forces. I was in charge of a department that, as a whole, was a department of the Government of the Republic of Croatia; i.e., a civilian department which controlled the armed forces in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Still, if we are trying to define the position that applies to other social communities, irrespective of the concrete situation in Croatia, would you say that it is normal and that the civilian authorities should, indeed, control the military?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. It would be bad if it was the other way around or if the army controlled itself. That army would be good for nothing. Or far be it from anybody for the military to control the civilian authorities. That would be bad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I listened carefully to the question put to you, and I listened even more carefully to your response. If I understand correctly, you're saying that the Ministry of Defence in Croatia was controlled by civilian political authorities, and if there were any military actions, they would be under the remit of political authorities. At the time of the events that unfolded that are mentioned in the indictment, the president was Mr. Tudjman, army general but also president of the Republic of Croatia. Would this mean that everything he may have done and everything that the HV may have done has always been, as far as you are concerned, controlled by the civilian political authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the supreme commander of the army has its authorities within the system of control and command, and you can't control him, as such. However, all the other segments in the army are under the control of the civilian authorities. In Croatia, for example, the government issued a decision on the reduction of the strength of the military. It was not the commander -- the supreme commander who issued that decision. It was the Croatian government that took into account its budgetary constraints and issued a decision for the Croatian Army to be reduced firstly by 30 per cent, then in the second period by a further 20 per cent. Therefore, a decision on the reduction in numbers was issued by the Ministry of Defence, and the Main Staff was just the operational segment that had to respect dead-lines and implement the decision on the reduction of the strength of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stream-line my question. It is an important question, in my view. And every time I put a question, remember, it is always an important question after four years of trial. If the Croatian Army intervened in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, does this mean, according to you, that this falls within the exclusive competence of the supreme commander, namely, at the time President Tudjman, or does this have to be approved by the civilian authorities, either the government, parliament, or the people, through elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll try and be even more careful in answering your question. The Croatian Army, with all of its elements that it had, did not intervene in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which means that it didn't send its formations as they existed and as they were. It never established a command structure that would have been in charge of all that. The Croatian Army at first, which was also the time when I joined, sent a group of officers to organise, prepare, and deploy forces which existed in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. During the war, there were some elements that belonged to the Croatian Army, but they were volunteers. The chain of command finished with the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council. Their command chain certainly did not go to the nearest operative command in Croatia or even the central command in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You must have noticed that when I put my question, I started off by saying "if," so this was a hypothetical question. And you answered by saying, if I have understood your answer correctly, you ascertain that the Croatian Army did not intervene in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is what you're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's exactly what I said, because when I think about the Croatian Army, I think about the organisational form, with all the elements belonging to it. For me, the organisational structure of the Croatian Army are not 100 or 150 men that arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and a majority of them were -- or 99 per cent were nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina who had fought in Croatia and then returned to their homeland. It's an entirely different thing, to my mind, than when we say Croatia and the Croatian Army. Let me tell you, in the month of October, we had 10.000 something -- I don't know the exact number. We had about 10.000 soldiers who hailed from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were absent for a reason, because they still had their status and there is only three in the Croatian military. If the HVO had been more active, they could have had two or three more brigades composed of such troops of volunteers. So when we say "the Croatian Army," then one has to take into account a system that is capable of performing a task, a system which has its head and a tail, it has its organisation in the command structure. Since we have touched upon that, let me tell you that those elements that found themselves around the borders between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, they pursued the principles of war because they opposed an army that would have consisted a whole in the Republic of Croatia, in its south, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was the OG-2 of the JNA under the command of General Strugar, and in Herzegovina the commander of one part was General Perisic, and in Croatia from Dubrovnik to Neum, the commanders were Admiral Zec and Jokic, I believe. So that was one military, a military that had taken an operative and strategic area and included Bosnia and Croatia, and from there it carried out maneuvers and attacks against the territory of the Republic of Croatia. In those cases, the Army of the Republic of Croatia did cross over the border into the territory that belonged to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, quite justifiably so, but it was not at the very beginning. It was only from November 1991. And then, on the 6th of December, 1991, when the Croatian Army finally took some 15 kilometres of the front-line south of Stolac, the so-called Stolovi, and then we called that area "TG-2," you will remember that, it was only then that the JNA forces did not manage to fool the defence of the Republic of Croatia which, up to then, exclusively defended itself in a narrow part of the Republic of Croatia; whereas, from its rear, from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was attacked by the forces of the JNA. And it was only when somebody realised that that territory of defence had to be extended 10 kilometres deeper into Herzegovina because those were the same forces, both in Croatia and Herzegovina. It was only then that it was stopped. They didn't manage to take Neum. They were stuck there for several months. And then in 1992, they were pushed back towards Dubrovnik. And in the month of October of that year, they were chased away to the territory of the then Yugoslavia, currently Montenegro. I believe that somebody else will ask me about that. I certainly hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rest assured, there will be other questions. Thank you for your answer, anyway, which, unless I'm mistaken, enables me to understand that you are saying that the Croatian Army intervened on a distance of 10 kilometres because of the action conducted by the JNA, but that on the 6th of December, 1991 - you are very precise - one should consider that the Croatian Army put an end to its action and did not take part in a military action in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which you define by giving us all its components. Have I summed up your position adequately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on the 6th of December, the Croatian Army stopped the advancement of the JNA from Stolac across a sector called "Stolovi," in the direction of Metkovic and the Neretva Valley, and along the Croatian literal [as interpreted] down to Neum, which means that on the 6th of December the JNA forces were finally stopped on that line and never again after that. Not only did they not cross that line, but also in the month of May 1992, the Croatian Army launched an offensive to push the JNA forces towards the very south of the Republic of Croatia. And then on the 15th of October - I believe that I am not mistaken about the date - the international community intervened. Your fellow countryman General Morillon conducted the negotiations between General Strugar and General Bobetko on the Invincible, and it was then agreed that the JNA would be given a possibility to retreat with dignity, that the Croatian Army would stop its advancement and allow them to retreat. And then the international community sent military observers on the border with Montenegro, which was in Yugoslavia at the time, and the peninsula of Prevlaka, and I had the honour, as a commander who had arrived in 1996, to co-operate with the military observers. Truth be told, they came to me, to my command post. I couldn't go to their command post, because their command post was in the area which was under the UN mandate, and not a single Croatian soldier, including generals, was allowed to go to that territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, to be very specific, on what date exactly did the HV, with its flags and banners and car license plates and soldiers, crossed over the border again of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? On what date, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian Army, that was sometime at the end of November 1991, after the fall of Slano, a place called Slano, and then Smokovljani and Visocani - it could not be defended in that narrow part because there were attacks from the flank - put part of its forces, let's say some 10 kilometres away from its border, to cover the area towards Stolac because the JNA was attacking from that axis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you're a specialist, and my questions are extremely specific. Try to answer my questions very specifically. My question was as follows: According to you, on what date, exactly, did the HV cross over the border again of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? That's my question. Either you know or you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'll tell you is this: In the second half of November -- now, what date it was exactly, I don't know, but it was 1991 -- I can't give you an exact date. That's the most I can do, because on the 15th of November I arrived in the Split Operative Zone, and then several days later -- but, anyway, on the 16th I came out onto the area where the JNA forces were stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood what you are saying, on the 1st of January, 1992 -- I'm just taking this date randomly. On the 1st of January, 1992, you state that in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, within its boundaries as part of the Yugoslav Federation, there wasn't a single soldier of the Republic of Croatia left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what I said. What I said is this: In that southern part in the second half of November 1991, it entered, and it stayed there right up until May 1992, when it moved from those positions towards the JNA and towards Dubrovnik to liberate the area. And then they penetrated 300 metres or 1 kilometre, depending on the configuration of the terrain, how far in depth they went, to allow them to stop the attacks coming from Eastern Herzegovina, or, rather, it was Bosnia and Herzegovina, because the Croatian Army, as it attacked along the borders, suffered onslaughts from the Serbian Army and the JNA until it withdrew from the flanks from Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that's how it had to position itself, and that's what General Beneta said, too. He was in that region along Popovo Polje right up until the hinterland of Dubrovnik. And now the Serb side always insisted on the Croatian Army withdrawing from that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so on the 6th of April, 1993, there were negotiations in Sarajevo, and the three commanders from Bosnia were invited, three of us. General Cervenko came on behalf of the Croatian Army to negotiate with Mladic, and then he said, When you withdraw from there, we will withdraw, too, from the 100 metres or 200 or 300 metres, because it's a narrow belt down there. So that's what happened, and that's how it stayed right up until -- well, I left the area, myself, by the Dayton Agreements. And then after the Dayton Accords, in that area, which is where the Croatian Army was, soldiers of the Croatian Defence Council entered because they were now the legal army in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So it's this Popovo Polje area that was taken over by the soldiers of the HVO, and in that way the Army of the Republic of Croatia was no longer in that part of the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petkovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, I'd just like to correct the transcript to avoid any misunderstandings. General, what was interpreted was that you stayed until Dayton. We're not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned the Dayton Accords, how did you link the Dayton Accords up?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian Army, in that border belt towards Dubrovnik, that is to say, this very narrow belt towards Dubrovnik, it stayed there -- it remained there at positions which entered into Bosnia-Herzegovina for a bit until the Dayton Accords, up to the Dayton Accords, because then the army of the Croatian Defence Council was sent into the area, which was then the legal army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Croatian Army left. So it was no longer down there; it was just along its border. And let me tell you that in 1996, in June, I, as the commander, was -- demobilised the last 1.000 soldiers of the Croatian Army and handed over the border to MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, thanks for your answers, which are now very specific. I think I understand that the Croatian Army stayed in a border area which was approximately 100 to 200 or 300 metres long. We're not going to measure this. The army remained in this border area until the Dayton Accords. And then after the Dayton Accords, the Croatian Army left the area and got replaced by the HVO; is this right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. And I think that after that, it was the MUP forces that arrived, because I met one of us here. It was Valentin Coric, actually. He was the chief of MUP of that district. And from the other side of the border, he deployed the forces of the civilian police there, so that the problem was definitely solved there, the civilian police on the Croatian side and the civilian police on the side of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, until the Dayton Accords, the international community knew that you were there in this border area, and it tried, together with the Serbs and the Muslims, to settle this issue. But clearly this issue was only settled after the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, you couldn't have any guarantees from the Army of Republika Srpska. That was the situation. You couldn't expect any guarantees from them as to what they would do at any point in time, because you just had the elevation from which you were defending yourselves, and if you left those positions you were in the sea. There was no depth, nothing. And let me just tell you of one particular detail. When the Yugoslav Army, in mid-October 1992, had to pull out pursuant to an agreement, then they thought up something, and that was that the Army of Republika Srpska should enter the region they had to leave, regardless of the agreement confirmed by General Morillon, so -- and that was the game they were playing. However, General Bobetko saw through that and arrived at that part of the border before them. And I think that they were pushed back towards Trebinje. And then the JNA forces and volunteers from Serbia were transferred to the Nevesinje and Bileca area, because had they lost the sea belt, they wanted to go back to the Neretva River. And in that case, we keep talking about Operation Bura, but nobody says why that was undertaken. Now, the volunteer forces from Serbia-Montenegro were transferred to the Eastern Herzegovina region to try and get back to the Neretva River Valley because they had lost the access to the sea when they had seized the territory of the Republic of Croatia, and that is why this Operation Bura that we keep mentioning had to be undertaken, to attack the concentration of these forces that had prepared to move forward, and that's when these forces were routed. The volunteer forces were very small in number in Eastern Herzegovina, anyway. I thought I was speaking slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, you see how it's very difficult to speak slowly. Now, to go back to General Antonetti's [as interpreted] question, does that mean that along that border belt of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian Army was there after the Washington Agreement was signed? Is that what that means?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction to the transcript. I'm not a general. I'd like this to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was told that I did not make a mistake, but I apologise if I misspoke anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So it was after the Washington Agreements. Now, the presence of the Croatian Army in that border belt of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for the Muslim side of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was that a problem of any kind for them?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, it was no problem at all. If you look at Sefer Halilovic's directive, then we can see that he wished to tie in the forces of the army in Herzegovina with the forces of the Republic of Croatia and plan to take Bileca with them, or, rather, Nevesinje, Bileca, and Trebinje, and in the western parts against -- towards Livno and Grahovo. And in his directive, he is tying in the forces as his right-hand neighbour, the forces of Croatia, and is counting on their support and reinforcement to take control of the Nevesinje, Bileca, and Trebinje area. That is what the directive was for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We've seen that directive here in the courtroom, and we studied it. But he referred to the Agreement on Friendship and Co-operation for the two neighbouring countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, General, give us the date of the document, Sefer Halilovic's directive for defence. What date was that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was September 1992. I can't remember the exact date, but we can take a look at it on the document and see.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I'm going to say it's 4D1240. That's the document number. It's not in your binder. The date of the document is the 10th of September, 1992, and it has the state of a sovereign exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, you also mention the Agreement on Friendship and Co-operation. Now, can you tell us what that agreement was? What kind of document was that, and when was the agreement reached and signed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The agreement was signed in July 1992. Whether it was the 21st of July, I'm not quite sure, 1992, as an inter-state agreement between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. Now, before that notes of goodwill -- of an intention of goodwill were exchanged, because Mr. Izetbegovic couldn't leave Sarajevo at the time, and this was the first time he left going to Zagreb to sign the Agreement on Friendship and Co-operation. And I think that in point 8 of that agreement, it talks about a joint enemy and an attack on Croatia from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there's mention of co-operation along the border between the two countries. And it was on the basis of this agreement that I became a member of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The HVO was recognised as a component part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll deal with that in due course. But one more question to you, General, as a professional soldier. For a professional soldier, where does -- at what point do you have the right to refuse to carry out an order? Where is that line drawn?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: At all times, if in complying I would be consciously committing a crime, and if the person who was conscious of his order being a crime, the person issuing it, and if I am conscious of the fact that if I were to carry out the order, I would be committing a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You've given us a lot of elements there, and it is a subject for a more extensive discussion, I would say. Perhaps we'll do that on some other occasion, but let's start off with the first topic that we decided to discuss during your testimony, and that is your arrival in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Yes. My colleagues tell me it's time for the break, so perhaps this is a good moment to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you are going to address this topic, we shall have the break now, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Court is back in session. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, we have so far used up 27 minutes, so I would like to ask you to be concise, and I also remind you to speak slowly because it would be a shame for the transcript not to record everything you said. To the question of Judge Antonetti, you have explained rather extensively the circumstances of your arrival in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is our following topic. I believe that we can start with a map right away, because that will be easiest. I would like to call document 4D2024. I don't know whether you have my binders next to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, when there is a new document, I've just discovered that we received three binders, but when there is a new document which hasn't been admitted, please tell us. Please say that it's a new document, a new exhibit, and in that case I can look more closely at those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we always mark the documents in your binders with stickers in two colours, yellow and orange, yellow for the documents that are not exhibits, orange for those that are. I believe it will be clear, and I hope no mistakes have been made. Moreover, in the lower half of the document, you will see a mark showing the status of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, can you see the documents in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You're looking at it on the screen. Tell us, General, do you know this map?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I know this map. I drew it, personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, what exactly does this map show?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this map I wanted to show you the connection between that part of the Republic of Croatia, where the zone of operations is, with the free area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So if you allow, I can comment what I have marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let us try and not describe the map, because it is all -- all markings are clearly explained. This southern part of Croatia, you say that the southern part of Croatia was occupied and that the HV had to enter BiH territory in order to defend Croatian territory. Show us which territory we are talking about. Perhaps we can enable the general to mark on the map.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you can see it. I'll mark it blue and place a "1" next to it [marks]. So this red stretch next to this blue marking is the southern part of Croatia which was occupied by the JNA with part of the VRS from Bosnia-Herzegovina. This round spot here [indicates] is the city of Dubrovnik, which was under siege, but it was not taken by the JNA. To the west - it isn't clearly visible, though - there's the line that the JNA and the VRS has been able to reach. That is close to Neum. That is the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina that is on the sea, and here there's the JNA and the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please place a number 2 next to the line where the JNA and the VRS were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now explain to us, General, when we say in this courtroom that this territory of Southern Croatia and the neighbouring area in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was not occupied, constitute a single theatre of war, what does that mean? And please circle it.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. This is the single theatre of war in which Operative Group 2 of the Army of Yugoslavia acted. It included the entire area of Eastern Herzegovina, the western parts of Montenegro, where JNA units were deployed, and the occupied part of the Republic of Croatia. This is a hole in which one force is active, and that is the JNA. It's the same forces in Croatia and outside of Croatia. These forces are under a single command, and this is called an operational strategic territory. The JNA called it "theatre of war." And there was the Groups of Operations number 2 with the Belgrade Corps, the Titograd Corps, and -- I don't need to enumerate them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In answering to Judge Antonetti's question, you said, General, that the Croatian Army stopped the onslaught of the JNA in late 1991. You mentioned the month of December in 1991. Is that the time when the events you marked with a number 2 happened?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I placed a number 2 next to it. I can also add, although it will be difficult to see, I can add an arrow above the number 2. This is the line where the offensive of the JNA was stopped [marks]. They were advancing on Croatian territory, and there were also forces from Bosnia-Herzegovina that attacked Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you are saying "from the flanks," please show this with arrows, and put a number 3 next to them.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So the number 3 represents attacks from the flanks by the JNA and the Serbian forces from Bosnia-Herzegovina against the Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from BiH territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, please place today's date on this map. It is the 11th of February, 2010.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like an IC number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in order to avoid that this document is rejected, you drew this map with colours, et cetera. This corresponds to the state of play exactly when; which month, which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this situation, I will mark here [marks], is that of the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When I look at this map, and if I'm mistaken, please correct me - you're free to do so - if I understand correctly, in December 1991 the JNA, in the area of the Operative Group 2, was launching an action aiming at occupying the entirety of the area circled in blue, with an added intention to seize Dubrovnik, and you have circled the city of Dubrovnik in blue as well. This would mean that if there had been successful, militarily speaking, the entirety of this area as well as the coastal area would have been under the control and the influence of the JNA, and as a result of this part of the Republic of Croatia's territory would have been cut off, especially the coastal area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right, Your Honour. Let me just add that in this situation as shown here, the JNA forces reached the Neretva and also controlled the eastern part of the city of Mostar. I may have drawn the line off the River Neretva. So they were on the banks of the Neretva. They held the east of Mostar and the southern part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Praljak, I believe it would be better for you not to intervene because we have General Petkovic testifying here, and any clarification or any changes can be done during the cross-examination by the Defence team of General Praljak, unless there is really a mistake. But I don't believe that is the case. So, Ms. Alaburic -- just a second. My colleague wants to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, I am still a little bit confused, because you have shown this map and commented on it, and it is supposed to be a view of a specific point in time, 6 December 1991. Now, as the map is drawn, the yellow part, which is South-Eastern Herceg-Bosna, and the coastal part, which is in pink, according to the legend, are areas already occupied by Serb forces. On the other hand, you have put two arrows pointing roughly in a south-western direction. But I do not understand. If that territory along the coast is already occupied by Serbs and the VRS, why should there be any operations planned? Perhaps you can clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was requested to show the directions of the succession of advancement. When the conquering of the south of Croatia started in October 1991, then operations began simultaneously here from this part and from up there, and that's how it went on until the 6th of December, 1991, when the entire area became a single occupied whole. Certainly, at that moment there was -- there were no more operations from the flanks. In early October 1991, it started -- attacks started from the south and from the flanks. On this day stated here, the entire area is controlled by the JNA, including the territory of Croatia. But most of the area in Bosnia-Herzegovina was controlled by the VRS because the JNA, due to a Security Council resolution, started pulling out of that territory in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to make sure that you actually confirm my conception, it is not entirely correct to put the date "6/12" for this whole map, because what the -- the arrows marked as number 3 refer to a previous period when they were still fighting to get to the coast. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. This started in mid-October 1991. There was an attack from the flank, followed by the next one, and then another attack. And then it all stopped, the attacks were stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you want an IC number?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a few more words about the map before we do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's be very precise. The date refers to the situation as it was on the territory of the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On that day, did this territory of the Republic of Croatia which is marked by pink, was it occupied by the JNA and the Serb force?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On that date, the 6th of December, 1991, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was still an integral state, there were no occupied territories?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was an integral state in Yugoslavia. I did not draw any occupied territories. I drew something that, in military terms, is called the theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we look at the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina alone, and if we look at the territory which is coloured orange, and the rest of the territory, which is not coloured, for which you said that it was a free territory, what could one say about such a division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and what period did that apply to?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: This was the situation in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. General, when you say "a free territory," what are you referring to? Is this the free territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the free territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the map, that part is not coloured.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who controlled that part of the territory?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: That territory was controlled by the BiH Army and the HVO or the Territorial Defence and the HVO, and it depended on the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please now be given an IC number for the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, I seem to get confused again and again. Now you have said -- I refer to page 42, line 9. The question was: "On that day, the 6th of December, 1991, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was still an integral state, there were no occupied territories?" And you say: "Yes." But if one looks at the map, Stolac definitely is in the area painted orange, which according to the legend is an area occupied by Serb and VRS forces. And you have then said that this refers to April 1992. Is there still another period covered by the map, or do you correct what you have said, that Bosnia and Herzegovina was entirely unoccupied on the 6th of December? It cannot very well be both, can it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on the 6th of December, 1992 [as interpreted], Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or, rather, in 1991, I apologise. The yellow part of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the area where the forces of the JNA were deployed, as they were pulling out from Croatia, as well as those that had pulled out of Slovenia, but that was still part of the Yugoslav territory. When Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed its independence, the pink territory became an occupied territory for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think the pink areas are not part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They are part of Croatia on this map. But it seems that you confirm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please do not interrupt me. It's not because it's impolite - I'm not so touchy - but it is because the interpreters lose what you say and what I say at the same time, so we have to apply some restraint. I may not always be correct, myself, and then I apologise. But the result of this exchange now is that you must correct the statement on page 42, line 9, 10, 11, 12, according to which, when you said that on the 6th of December the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, apart from the fact that it did not really, as such, exist then, was still an integral state, there were no occupied territories, that was wrong, correct, or the map is wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, correct, that was an integral state. And this yellow territory was where JNA units were deployed, those that were pulling out from Croatia and previously from Slovenia. When Bosnia and Herzegovina proclaimed its independence in April 1992, and when they proclaimed the JNA a hostile army, the yellow territories, as they are drawn here, became occupied areas for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I will not -- I will not insist now, but it seems a bit confused, I must say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could you please allow me to do my job properly and bring my examination about the map to an end, and then everything will become clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This date, 6th December 1991, refers to what you marked by numbers 1, 2, and 3 on this map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now be given an IC number for the map, and then we will put another clean copy of the map, and then we will discuss the map in the light of a different date, the 6th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could give an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I still need the map. Ms. Alaburic, now, you've said the 6th December refers to 1, 2, and 3, but a short while ago the general accepted on my question that number 3 refers not to the 6th of December, but for a period previous to the 6th of December. I'm not pleased with your observation that we are hindering your examination, because there are contradictions which the Chamber must clarify. I'm sorry. And you have again contributed to the confusion, I'm sorry to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, very well, I apologise. Well, let's take things one at a time. Your Honour, the problem is I'm losing my minutes on your questions, and I'm not going to be able to do what I planned to do. And my analyses show that I have to spend about 20 to 25 per cent of my time to follow up on the Judges' questions, which prevents me from working the way I should. That's why I intervened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Number 3, General, shows the axis and directions of actions that resulted in an occupation as it was on the 6th of December, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could we please be given an IC number for this map, and then I am going to call up for a clean copy of the same map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to give an IC number, but I have a question to ask. So please give an IC number, and then I'll ask the question.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The marked version of Exhibit 4D02024 shall be given Exhibit IC01173. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. General Petkovic, based on this map, you have let us know how, according to you, the JNA and the Serbian forces were positioned on the 6th of December, 1991. And you gave us loads of details, and this is all in the transcript. And upon the request of your counsel, you also pointed out that the JNA had positions in the coastal areas, and they had taken up those positions in October. And you put the number 3 there. That's all very well. However, we have to look at the words that are used, because as a legal expert, I have to make sure that the correct language is used. When we talk about occupied areas, "occupied" has a legal connotation, of course. And unless I'm mistaken, on the 6th of December, 1991, from an international point of view, we had a Yugoslav federation made of several socialist republics which were members of this federation. Therefore, the All People's Army or the JNA, in December 1991, while the Republic of Croatia was not recognised internationally, nor was it the case for the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so I would like to know if I'm mistaken in saying that the JNA deployed its forces in areas which belonged to the territory of the Yugoslav state. And I'm using the word "deployed," and not "occupied."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's how one could say, strictly speaking, and looking at the period up until Croatia proclaimed its independence on the 15th of January, 1992, or, rather, when it was recognised as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if we use military jargon, we have to use the word "deployed"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if troops are deployed as a result of combat, then you can't use the term "deployment." Deployment is something that is done peacefully, freely, and you just send troops to certain areas. That's deployment. However, if you start from the border and engage in combat, then this is not deployment.
