And although Croatia was still officially part of Yugoslavia, the JNA carried out attacks against the forces which were deployed in the area, which were mostly the police forces of the Republic of Croatia. So we can't be talking about peaceful deployment of the kind practiced by an army in peacetime. It was combat, irrespective of the fact that it was still the territory of their common state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I fully understood what you say. But to clarify this point, I'll take an example. Let's assume that today, in the Republic of Croatia, part of the territory is facing some problems, and the new president, and unless I'm mistaken it's Ivo Josipovic, the new president decides that the Croatian Army will position itself on those territories, where there will be some strife or something happening. According to you, do you think that the Croatian Army would deploy itself or would occupy those territories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian Army would be deployed in such areas. However, if to do that it had to engage in combat, then that area would be placed under control by military action. Deployment is free and peaceful, and if, on the other hand, there is something that I'm not happy with, then I engage in action. When, on the 6th of December, the JNA torched the entire Konavle Valley and did in Dubrovnik what they did, it is not deployment. It is not in the spirit of what our -- the militaries do to deploy their troops. This is an entirely different matter. The JNA did not arrive and deploy its troops in six, eight, or ten locations in the south of Croatia, but rather they had engaged in combat for several months using the territories of both the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then on the 15th of January, when independence was proclaimed and when the JNA was still there, it became an occupational force from what could have been a force that only deployed its troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, please focus. On the 15th of January, 1992, did Croatia proclaim its independence or was it internationally recognised on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, Croatia was internationally recognised. Its moratorium expired sometime in the month of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: October?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, October. And according to that --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Hold on, hold on, hold on. I'll take things one at a time. When we speak about the three-month moratorium, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what it means? When was it that Croatia actually proclaimed its independence, and what is the meaning of the term "Croatian moratorium"?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Croatia, I believe it was in June that Croatia proclaimed its independence, and then, at the incitement of the international factors to have the situation resolved more easily, allegedly, that that should be frozen for a period of three months.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, when you say "June," what year is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And was it then that the presidents of the former Yugoslavia, pursuant to a proposal from the international community, that they decided about the independence of Slovenia and Croatia, to freeze that for three months, their independence, in order to achieve some agreement, and that was the moratorium; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, officially, what is the official date of independence for the Republic of Croatia? Is it the 8th of October?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, the 8th of October is Independence Day for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Therefore, General, since when was the Republic of Croatia an independent state?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: From the 8th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army, on the territory of the Republic of Croatia in December 1991, can it be considered to have been an occupational army then?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I apologise for the misunderstanding earlier on. The 8th of October, the day Croatia was declared independent, is when the attack started; in 1991, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to that same map that we were dealing with a moment ago, and I'm interested, General, in what the situation was like in April 1992. So we're now going to speak about April 1992. The parts of the territory of the Republic of Croatia coloured pink here, and we're just referring to the territory in the Split Operations Zone, was that territory under the occupation of the JNA, or, rather, the forces of the Croatian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, they were under occupation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, on the -- or, rather, in the month of April 1992, the territory in orange or yellow, was that territory under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army and the forces of the Bosnian Herzegovinian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was it exactly. That territory was controlled by the VRS and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, please, could you tell us whether, at the beginning of April 1992, you had any knowledge about any combat plans of the Yugoslav People's Army and the forces of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian Serbs? And if so, could you draw that in on this map, please?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The forces of the Yugoslav People's Army and the army of the Bosnian Serbs, in April 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 1992, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1992, undertook the implementation of a plan that had been devised previously at the level of the JNA, and it meant this: From the west, Kupres, Livno, Tomislavgrad --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Might we provide the general with a felt-tipped pen so that he can mark this in on his screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to draw a circle 'round that territory [marks]. And then they moved across Herzegovina down the Neretva River Valley, and another branch towards the Republic of Croatia and Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, could you put a number 1 for this plan of invasion, plan of occupation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks] The second part of the plan was for the forces located in the Neretva River Valley to continue the advancement towards Ploce, Metkovic, Makarska, that is to say, Croatia, and another branch to continue and link up with the forces -- to continue the advancement and link up with the forces coming in from the western part, Livno, Tomislavgrad, and Kupres, who were moving eastwards [marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, could you put a number 2 for those axes?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And let's state this once again. What period are we talking about for these plans?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: It was April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, had these plans been carried out, what would have happened to the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The Republic of Croatia south of Split would also have been occupied, just as the southern-most part of the Republic of Croatia, which means the entire region south of Split would have been under the occupation of the JNA and the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in that area, would the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the free territory of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would it border on the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it would not. The territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina would also have been cut across, cut off, and the corridors from -- well, north of Mostar, Posusje, would have been an enclave under siege in the Central Bosnia-Herzegovina, without any access to any of the states surrounding it, which in this case is just one, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions on this map. Now, before I tender it into evidence or ask for a number, do you have any questions? If not, may I have an IC number for this map, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we have an IC number for this map, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The second marked version of Exhibit 4D02024 shall be given Exhibit IC01174. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question, General Petkovic. We have just seen two maps in quick succession. You've explained how the JNA took up its position and how the troops were positioned on the ground. I assume that your counsel will ask for these two maps to be admitted. Can you tell me, according to you, in what way these maps are relevant to understand the military situation resulting from the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, based on the indictment raised and the assertions made with respect to the involvement of the Army of the Republic of Croatia with the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this map is highly relevant. The situation in the Republic of Croatia was tied in with the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The general territory between the two red occupied territories in the Republic of Croatia was not [indiscernible] by Croatian forces, but for moral and psychological relationships towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, not to be considered closed off, but the defence was based on joint resistance to the Serb forces and the Yugoslav People's Army. Now, these events, from April 1992 onwards, in the west, which is number 1, I showed the direction taken by the forces, and then later on, with the liberation of the eastern part from Neretva to Stolac, the liberation of East Mostar, in my view, led to a joint agreement between President Izetbegovic and President Tudjman, and an Agreement on Friendship and Co-operation which was reached. And in point 4, it emphasizes the need for trans-border military co-operation, because it was noted that both Bosnia-Herzegovina -- that Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia had come under attack exclusively from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that Croatia was being attacked from BH, and that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, just a few days after independence had been proclaimed, did not have the necessary number of troops to help the Republic of Croatia to repel and prevent attacks by Serb forces on Croatian territory and thereby to block entry into Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, these events, which took part in the first part -- took place in the first part of 1991, tells us that Croatia did not have its own interest, but the joint interest was to stand up to a joint adversary in the trans-border region, the border belt between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, this is a question I'm putting to you and which I shall not put to you again. It might be the most crucial question. To understand the indictment, should one only look at the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH, or should one consider this conflict including the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, looking at Bosnia-Herzegovina, and only the conflict there between the HVO and BH, would not be complete. You mustn't leave the Serbs out from this equation and from the overall conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That means that they are the ones who must be considered a component of the conflict, and not to leave them aside and then just look at the conflict between the HVO and the BH. Why? Because the part of the territory that we are looking at now, we have, on the one side, the Serbs doing what they're doing, occupying territory and so on, and on the other side you have the HVO and the BH Army and certain other forces of the Republic of Croatia helping them to stand up to the Serb aggression and to prevent the closing off the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, therefore, jeopardising -- thus jeopardising the Republic of Croatia. So all three sides are linked up. You can't exclude the Serbs in this equation. Had there not been the Serbs, there wouldn't have been any need for activities on the part of the HVO, BH, and so on. We would just be sitting in Geneva and negotiating. Everybody would have waited for the negotiations to end, and nobody would have resorted to rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's move on. We'll skip the next map in your binder, and let's look at P162 now, please, which is an order dated the 16th of April, 1992, from Commander Janko Bobetko, on the establishment of a forward command post and southern front in Grude. Tell us, General, does this order have anything to do with the map we've just looked at for April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it has an important connection. Because of the situation, the forward command post was set up in Grude, which, since the forces were less well organised in this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it took on the role of the organiser for the establishment of these forces, for deploying them along the lines, and for commanding the troops in the battles against Republika Srpska and the JNA, and that is the sole reason that the forward command post in Grude was set up in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, which is P163. It is also an order from Commander Janko Bobetko about the composition of the command at the forward command post at Grude. And, General, you are stipulated here under item 1?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. Now, this is -- these are the specifics, listing the names of the people making up the command post. And there were a total of 11 of us, and those people were responsible for these and forthcoming expected operations in this territory in April, May, and June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, when did you arrive in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I arrived on the 14th, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: "The 14th," meaning what month?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The 14th of April, 1992. And I was officially recorded as being there on the first -- next day, on the 15th. So the first day was sort of reconnaissance, but I always list the actual date of my arrival, although I actually took up my duties on the 15th. So it would have been more correct to say, perhaps, the 15th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, in arriving in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you expect any main staff to exist over there or anything like that, any HVO Main Staff, or the Main Staff of any other Croatian and Muslim forces? What did you actually expect to find?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was told that a main staff existed. I didn't know in what shape or form. But I was told that as it was, the Main Staff, from the 4th to the 10th of April, commanded the HVO force in the battles against the JNA and the Serb forces at Kupres, Tomislavgrad, and Livno, and we did expect to find this Main Staff in place. However, what happened was that the man who headed it and some other men had left, allegedly to return. However, I actually never saw them. And let me just add that I was surprised, upon my arrival in the area, to see that the BH authorities, south of the line running from Prozor to Jablanica, which is a long line of Eastern and Western Herzegovina, the central authorities had no operative command. It had no units whatsoever, except for an independent battalion in Mostar. So in that respect, I was really surprised to find that, because I had expected at least two or three brigades of the Territorial Defence, but there was nobody there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, what about Herceg-Bosna? What existed of Herceg-Bosna in that area when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, Your Honours: If I were to be asked about that particular day, I can tell you that I couldn't find my bearings at all and I didn't know anything. It was only later on, after the 24th -- after the fighting in Livno, that I sat down and talked to Jozo Maric, discussed the situation. He was the head in Grude. He was a professor, and he explained to me about Herceg-Bosna, which was an organisation of Croats for the defence of the territory. He said, We have these troops in the municipalities and so on. And then I asked him, All right, now Boban and the others, who else was there? Well, they couldn't point to anybody. Anything that was said, they would say, That's Boban, the HDZ, the Presidency, nobody around him allegedly leading the HVO. And around him you, you had three men in a hotel in Grude. Now, I expected in those first 10 days that I would meet at least 15 people who meant something, but, no, that wasn't the case. I had the feeling that Boban was quite alone in all that territory, so that I wasn't acquainted with the structure, I never saw any of the people that made it up until, say, August 19 -- well, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, your answer is an important one, and it merits one spending time on it. On the 16th of April, 1992, you go to the forward command post in Grude because there is going to be fighting with the Serbs. And when you arrive there, you say, I thought that there was a staff of the HVO, and there was nothing there. You don't see a single HVO member anywhere. Then after the fighting in Livno, you talk to Mr. Maric, who talks to you about the HVO and who says that there is Mate Boban. When I listened to you, I had the feeling that before the 16th of April, 1992, you had had no contact whatsoever with Mate Boban and all the people from the HVO, and now, in this instance, you are discovering that it actually exists after the fighting has taken place. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, not exactly. In late March 1992, while with a team from the Split Zone of Operations, I visited the area, the areas that were shown in red where the Serb attack was stopped, by mere chance at a hotel in Metkovic, I ran into Mate Boban. My assistant for logistics from the zone of operations stood up and greeted the man. They were hugging each other, and he introduced him to me as Mr. Boban and introduced me to him as Mr. Petkovic, the operations officer in our zone. That's how we met and sat down, and then I drew my conclusions from the ensuing conversation. This assistant of mine was a manager of a hotel chain in Split, whereas Mate Boban was the manager of a company -- of a wholesale company in Imotski, and they did business together. And I believe that Boban's brother was also in logistics in the navy. The conversation took about an hour, and we spoke. What the situation was like here, will Neum fall, what will happen, those were his questions. And I asked him to tell us what kind of forces can be found along the Neretva from Capljina to Mostar on which we were leaning, in Croatia, as forces that could provide security to us, and that's how the conversation ran. And then at one point he said, You commanded the defence at Sibenik. It would be good if you could come to help us out and see what kind of structure we have and what kind of forces we have. And I said, No problem, I can come and visit for two or three days and see what you have set up, and it would be good if I could meet two or three of your people who know something about that. He insisted on me coming to join their ranks, but I didn't. That's when we met first. We never spoke about Herceg-Bosna at the time or anything else. He told me that the Croats organised themselves by municipalities, whichever way they thought fit or were able to implement, and he needed someone with experience, because in the war in Croatia I commanded the defence of Sibenik, I was in the zone of operations. And that's where we broke off. After three or five days, three of their men arrived who worked for the defence and gave us information about where the HVO was, what they had, et cetera. My following contact was a phone conversation, when Kupres came under attack. I believe it was on the 4th of April, 1992, when he requested help from the zone of operations, but we were unable to provide it. We were just saying we were monitoring the situation and see what was happening. Those are my contacts with him in 1992. I met him for the first time when we spoke for about an hour at the hotel in Metkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document we have before us, those 11 people who are mentioned, under point 7 I see that this is a civilian by the name of Bruno Stojic. Is it the same Bruno Stojic who is sitting here in the courtroom? And if that's the case, why is the term "civilian" used for someone in the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, indeed, under 7 there is "Bruno Stojic." It is stated that he's a civilian. He was charged with the logistics in this forward command post. As far as I know, for some time prior to that he was involved in some logistical activities which were under the authority of that Main Staff that was or was not in existence, and everybody else, except for the last person mentioned, were considered members of the Main Staff, and they are all the people from the Main Staff I met. The chiefs had gone to Zagreb or wherever, and I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This civilian by the name of Bruno Stojic, who was in charge of logistics, was this someone whom you knew already or was it someone you met in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I only met him then. Except for the person under 2, Jure Zadro, I met him sometime in late March or early April. And I met Zarko Keza at the same time as Zadro, because Boban had sent them off to Ploce to present the situation in Herzegovina to us. I didn't know the others, except for number 11 because he was from the Croatian Army also.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, when you went to Bosnia-Herzegovina, if we disregard the JNA officers who worked there and who you didn't know them, did you know anybody else in Herzegovina; relatives, business partners, anybody close to you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I knew nobody in Herzegovina. In my military career, as far as Bosnia is concerned, I was in Sarajevo and in Kalinovik, and it took me -- or, rather, I travelled through Mostar when I travelled from Sarajevo. I spent 15 minutes at the bus station there and continued. That's all I know about Bosnia-Herzegovina, although I was a soldier for 23 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you went to Bosnia-Herzegovina, sir, did you have your own concept of the internal structure of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: My concept? I never thought about these things, because it wasn't for me to do so, nor did anybody care to hear my opinion. But I did hear that the leaders of Bosnia-Herzegovina talked, and I thought that it would be best for them to accept what the international community was offering them in 1992 and 1993, because at that time solutions for the situation in that country were being put forward then. Three peoples lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I thought that each people must have the same rights, irrespective of their share in the overall population. And that, to my mind, would have been a well-ordered state. Anything else, I thought, would not have been a good outcome, because the one with lesser rights would not have been satisfied. But they could've reach any agreement at all. If they had decided to turn Bosnia-Herzegovina into a monarchy, it would have been fine by me. I would have saluted that king.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, if I understand you well about -- or, rather, you mean to you, as a professional soldier, any solution the leaders of the three constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina come up with would have been all right with you, even a monarchy?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, even today.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, let's be brief, General, because we have heard much about these things in this courtroom before. Were the attempts to stop the onslaught of the VRS around Livno successful?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 24th of April, 1992, a large operation of the VRS and the JNA still at the time was launched, focusing on the town of Livno and the municipality of Livno, but also on the remoter parts of the municipality of Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, to Janko Bobetko, what was the most important thing at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was extremely important to him to stop the Serbs at lines beyond Livno at any cost. The fall of Livno-Tomislavgrad were not an option. That's why orders were given that the towns of Livno-Tomislavgrad be provided with concrete blocks to make impossible traffic along the roads. So Janko Bobetko was determined to stop the attacks of Livno, because that would have -- that meant making impossible further attacks on Herzegovina and on the parts of Croatia south of Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, under these circumstances, was it possible to start considering the liberation of Dubrovnik and the occupied part of Southern Croatia that we saw on the map?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, by no means, because any effort to liberate Dubrovnik and the other territory we saw on the map, with someone being in the position to attack you from behind was, militarily, not an option, so we first had to do what I've just mentioned and then go south toward Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The towns you mentioned, General, were not recorded in the transcript. You're speaking too fast. When you say "attack you from behind," which territory do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about Croatia, the towns of Split, Makarska, Ploce, all the way to Metkovic; that is, the Neretva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Which liberation actions were organised in that period? We are now referring to May and June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: After remedying the situation in the area of Livno-Tomislavgrad, and setting up a firm line of defence, which can also be termed a major defeat of the VRS and the JNA, it was General Bobetko's assessment that at the moment when the JNA, in May, started leaving the territory of BiH, in a way, and handing over authorities to local forces, and those who belonged to the JNA but crossed over to those local forces, he assessed that was a convenient moment to do something and undertake an offensive action while they are re-positioning their forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in one sentence, which area was liberated.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The eastern banks of the Neretva River from the town of Capljina to Mostar, the eastern part of Mostar, Bijelo Polje, the Dubrava Plateau, and the municipality of Stolac. Some parts of that municipality, we were not able to liberate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at the following document, P279.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I've been listening to you carefully. And based on the documents that we had had, I seem to understand the following: The Serb forces occupy the Dubrovnik area, and this causes a great deal of an issue for the Croats. In military terms, General Bobetko is launching a military action in sector Mostar, Bijelo Polje, the Dubrava Plateau, as well as the municipality of Stolac, in order to take up positions and to allow the Croatian Army in the area of Dubrovnik -- to allow this army to fail any attempt of the JNA. And in April 1992, there is a military operation that is directed against the Serbs. This is what I seem to understand from what you're saying. But in the indictment, which I'm sure you've read, you are aware that the Prosecutor claims that you were part of a JCE with General Bobetko, and in fact this joint criminal enterprise had the following purpose: either to take the control of municipalities by ethnic cleansing, and so on and so forth. I'm not going to go into the details. Based on that, one could think that in 1992, the forward command post in Grude was part of this plan. And here you are giving us an explanation of a military nature. So to summarise, you're saying to us that the Croatian Army, in April 1992, had only one objective; namely, to launch a military action against the Serbs. And if I understand the way you're looking at this, the question of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or anything to do with Muslims was not really the main purpose of this action. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, you're absolutely right, this is exactly how it was. When we liberated the eastern bank of Neretva, Mr. Izetbegovic proclaimed a state of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on that day we gave him a gift of a large part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, some 70 kilometres' long and 30 kilometres' wide, from Capljina to Stolac. That was the largest area that was liberated in 1992 and 1993 from the Army of Republika Srpska and the remains of the JNA. After these events, General Bobetko continued acting in the territory of the Republic of Croatia towards Dubrovnik and liberated the southern part of the Republic of Croatia, and the HVO, which had already acted in concert with the 1st Brigade of the BiH Army, took it upon itself to secure the newly-liberated line in the newly-liberated area. In July 1992, General Bobetko withdrew elements of the Croatian Army from that territory and deployed them in the direction of Dubrovnik. The only group that remained was the TG-2, which changed sides every three months. And let me say just one more thing. After the operations which were carried out in the southern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to be more specific, in the eastern part of Herzegovina, which were all either actions to liberate the territory or to defend the territory, there was a meeting between Tudjman and Izetbegovic which resulted in an agreement on co-operation and friendship. I believe that Mr. Izetbegovic would not have come to Zagreb if he thought that somebody had occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he would not have signed the agreement on co-operation with the Republic of Croatia in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, according to what you know, the engagement of the Croatian Army on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, did it have even the least note of animosity or hostility towards the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No. On the contrary, Muslims also participated in those operations, together with the Croats and the Croatian Army and the Croats in the HVO. Therefore, all militarily-capable men who wanted to do so took up arms and joined the operation. Do you think that the 30 per cent of the Muslims who were in the HVO would have participated in those operations if they didn't want to? They would have said, No, we don't want to wage a war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, you see how difficult it can be for an international judge. If we had before us the documents of the Main Staff, the Croat Main Staff, documents dealing with all operations under the remit of General Bobetko, given the case that you're putting forward here, namely, Dubrovnik and what happened there, perhaps a reasonable judge would have better understood the situation if they had everything before them. Unfortunately, as I've already said, we only have what is given to us, what the Prosecutor is lodging, what the Defence teams are lodging, and based on that we have to ask questions, question that are intricate, that are very sensitive sometimes, and, in fact, we have some pieces of the puzzles that are missing. And to really be very precise, General Petkovic, in this sort of case when you have military operations being carried out, as far as I'm concerned, we should have all documentations dealing with the Croatian Army as well as all documentations regarding the VRS and the JNA, as well as all the documents from the BiH. And I believe that it's after having looked at all those documents that we could really shed some light and see the truth. But if we have only part of those documents, only part of the truth, only part of the facts will be known and it will be very difficult to find one's way through this. And this is why sometimes I'm asking you long questions, because I'm trying to fill some voids. Sometimes -- well, I remember that the issue of Dubrovnik was mentioned at the beginning of the trial by General Praljak, and there were some objections from the Prosecution and I didn't quite understand what was at stake there, and now I listen to you and I understand better. And, of course, I would have understood even better if I had before me all the documents from the Main Staff of the Croatian Army, as well as all the documents from the JNA, and anything relating to General Mladic as well. So, unfortunately, I don't have all this, and so, please, I apologise if sometimes my questions are long, but I'm trying to uncover the truth and sometimes it's very complicated. Ms. Alaburic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's look at P279, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. I just observe, and it's the second time, Mr. Praljak sending a message to Ms. Alaburic, who is not his counsel. Communication is possible between an accused and his counsel, but not with an accused and other counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, we do take issue with that. There is no restriction on that. He is perfectly entitled to do that. He can do it through his counsel to us or he can communicate to us. There simply is nothing in principle, in the Rules, in any sort of practice to prevent that. Provided it's done politely and not disruptively, he should be entirely free to communicate information to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think he ought to do that through counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps that could, in practice, conveniently be done, but we maintain our position, Your Honour. It's not -- unless there is some security implication, which is another matter altogether, Your Honour, he is entitled to do that. And I would say this, Your Honour: Then, we would invite a ruling on that, because that is our firm position. And if the Trial Chamber is going to rule against us on that, then we do wish to have that very clearly indicated, either unanimously or by a majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The Chamber will deliberate about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the record, I would like to support what my learned friend has just said. I would also like to remind you that this has been a communication problem all the time. We, from the Praljak Defence team, have discussed that, and every time we need to communicate about a mistake in the record, some imprecision in questions that were put, we discuss whether General Praljak would call the special usher, who would then come to Mr. Praljak, and then the usher would come to me, and then I would send that to Ms. Alaburic. I think it's unnecessary, because there is no ban on communication between Defence teams, and we believe that we are free to communicate. If you intend to impose a ban, I believe you should state clear reasons for that, and we will abide by the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, I would like to share my position on that with you. General Petkovic wants to say something. Maybe he should be given the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wouldn't talk about that. I would like to answer your previous questions about the documents. I can claim that most of the documents already exist, and we have complete documentation for the liberation of the east bank of the Neretva, from the initial order to the last order. We've also demonstrated from the same time, I believe, two or three orders issued by General Perisic or, rather, the Army of Yugoslavia. So some of the documents have already been tendered. The only one that is not is the one issued on the 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, about the communication, I believe that this is an important issue, and I think it's good that Judge Trechsel shared his position with us. I can tell you what my position is. And I personally handed over a paper to General Praljak containing a note on something that I deemed relevant, and my reason for that was this: If I have reached an agreement with a Defence team that we can communicate freely and that that communication does not necessarily have to go through the Defence lawyer of the accused that we want to address, that we can take a short-cut in communication, as it were. I would consider it inappropriate that if somebody communicates with an accused without a previous consent with their Defence team, and it is part of our legal ethic, but if the Trial Chamber wishes us to communicate only with our peers, who will then be mediators in our communication with the accused, then I will abide by that decision and I will apologise for my previous communication with the other accused, including Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that we have to thank the contributions by Mr. Stewart and also Ms. Alaburic and others. And as it was already stated, the Chamber will deliberate on this matter, and of course it will make its decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In view of that, it might be good to hear what the Prosecution has to say to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until further notice, I'm still the Presiding Judge in this Trial Chamber, and so I will give the floor to Mr. Scott. And, Mr. Scott, I was going to ask you what was your point of view on all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was really going to hold my fire on this, just as a matter of peace in the courtroom. But since so much has been made of it and since the Court has now said that it's going to actually deliberate on the matter, I think the Prosecution has to then, in these circumstances, make at least one or two observations. And I say this with some reluctance, but given the issue that was raised earlier today and some of the things that have been said and some of the pleadings filed in the last two days, I do have to note the Prosecution has raised a number of times that many of these examinations -- many of the relationships are very friendly ones and friendly examinations, and when the Defence continually protest that we are all single, individual units that don't co-operate with each other and have their own individual interest, this flies a bit in the face of that. I fully understand that they're entitled to co-operate, to a reasonable degree. I understand that. That's common sense. But I do want to note for the record, and if the Court is going to deliberate on this, I think it's rather noteworthy. It's a little bit akin to Mr. Praljak passing a note and saying, Here, ask this question. That sound like the sort of independence that we're sometimes led to believe. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I just comment on that, Your Honour, that, actually, one needs to look bit carefully at what Mr. Scott has just said, because in principle, he is supporting our position. That's quite clear. He's having a little bit of a complaint about where it leads, and he's having a little bit of a whinge about what we said about previously filings and so on, but he is basically supporting our position. He doesn't say anything to suggest that there is anything, in principle, which prevents us from having this sort of communication, and that is, in fact, quite clear from what he's just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I hope that some of our friends from the OTP can confirm that whenever I noticed a Prosecutor misrepresenting a document or having any problem with a document, I sent an e-mail to my colleague from the OTP to draw their attention to that so that they didn't have to be publicly admonished. I believe that it was a friendly gesture. And if I do the same thing vis-à-vis my colleagues in the Defence teams, that doesn't change the fact that my accused is independent -- that my client is an independent person, enjoying all the rights as if he were tried independently. And as for the remark that Praljak suggests questions that I should put, I hope that Mr. Scott did not mean it seriously, because I believe that Mr. Scott knows that I don't need anybody to suggest questions to me and what I should ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not going to belabour it any further. I just -- I do want to respond to Mr. Stewart, who I have great respect for, but I don't appreciate him talking about the Prosecution whinging. And as to the characterisation of my comments, the words speak for themselves. I'll leave it to the Chamber, but I do not want them to be characterised by Mr. Stewart as what I agree with or don't agree with. I simply made the observation for the record, as invited by the Chamber, and I did think it was something that had to put on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I can withdraw the word "whinge." I've corrupted my language with adopting an Austro-Asian word. I'll substitute "complaint" for that. It wasn't intended in the least bit offensively, but it is a legitimate point that, in fact, it has been a complaint about other things. That's neither here or there, but I'll take the word back. It wasn't meant impolitely at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was actually time to have the break. The Trial Chamber will confer, and after the break we will give you the position of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will hand down its decision regarding the communication between an accused and other counsel. The Trial Chamber states that an accused cannot address any kind of communication to other counsel, only to his counsel, and the latter will decide whether that information has been to be passed on to other Defence counsel, who will then pass it on to their client. In short, if Mr. Praljak has something to tell the other Defence counsel, he should address this to his counsel. That is why there is somebody there whose role is to pass on the messages. And his counsel will then see how this can be passed on to his colleagues. Have you understood, Mr. Praljak? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I have understood your decision, and of course it is a final decision, having been taken by the Trial Chamber. However, every time I need to hand over a message that I consider to be important, in the sense of allowing the right decisions to be made in this trial, I'm going to ask for a break to see whether they have read the message, to give them time to read it and consider it, and then afterwards to be able to hand it over to the next Defence team, which will also need a few minutes to read through the note. So I have to respect the ruling, of course, but unfortunately I have noticed, and with the Court's permission I'd like to be allowed to say, that at this Tribunal and in this trial, decisions are being made to the detriment -- great detriment, in my opinion, of the fairness of this trial, and that prejudices are being formed, and I will give this some thought and decide what steps I'm going to take, if any. And I'll be able to inform Your Honours when the conflict began between the Judges and others, and how certain military matters are being discussed, and why there isn't a military expert here throughout, because there is a great lack of knowledge when it comes to military matters, generally speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Praljak. In future, turn to your counsel, give them your comments, and they will deal with it. Like that, this kind of problem will not arise. Let's resume, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, third try. Let's go to P279. Third go. Third time lucky. Now, this document is signed by you and is titled "Preliminary Report," and my question to you is: Did you write this text?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this text was written by three people; by myself and two of my associates.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what services were these associates of yours from?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: There weren't many services at the time, but Zarko Keza was an intelligence officer throughout, and Mr. Zadro, as the senior person, was the communications man, but he held the highest rank, and he was in the JNA previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, did you deliver this preliminary presentation or introductory presentation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was never presented because I wasn't provided with the right information as to what was actually the object of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what did you think your role ought to be at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The information that reached me told me that -- led me to believe that I was to chair the meeting and that I was the person to choose the topics. That was the information I had, as far as preparations for this meeting were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, and who was supposed to attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting was supposed to be attended by Mr. Boban, General Bobetko, and the commanders of three -- well, three to four commanders of the municipal staffs of this region along the Neretva River, and two or three people from the South-East Herzegovina Operations Group. So that would make a total of 35 to 40 people overall.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, was Arif Pasalic supposed to be at the meeting, as commander of the Mostar unit of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the delegation from Mostar brought Mr. Pasalic with it as battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when did you learn that the meeting was not going to be the kind of meeting that you thought it was going to be?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting started, I think, at 4.00 p.m. in Medjugorje, and sometime between 1.00 and 2.00 General Bobetko arrived. He arrived after talking to Boban. He came to see me. That's where the forward command post was. And he asked me whether I was prepared for the meeting. On the wall, there was a large map, 1:25.000 was the scale, and he said -- and I said it couldn't have been a better map and that the written document would be typed out shortly. And when we received the written document, the general took a look at it, and he said to me, Do you think that I'm going to sit in the front row while you chair the meeting? And I said, Well, that was the information I received. And then he said, The meeting is a military meeting. I'm not interested in any of the civilians. They have Mr. Boban, so they can discuss it with him, and I don't have time to spend an hour and a half at a meeting like that. Then he looked at number 2 -- item number 2 and said that there was no need to discuss the matter, especially since at that time the HVO had no documents, so we couldn't discuss the establishment of brigades or anything without any documents governing that type of organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So what was your actual role at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was defined -- my role was defined as being the first person to present the military situation in the territory east of the Neretva River, including Stolac, Capljina, East Mostar, or, rather, the lines facing the Army of Republika Srpska, and I would do this by pointing out the exact positions on the map, to give the exact number of soldiers, who they belonged to, and the support system in general, with the exact number of tanks and everything else. And I also had the task of assessing what the -- what Serb forces we would encounter in front of us. So that was my task, and I was supposed to present that information at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, whether that is what you did. Or, rather, did you have a written speech or did you speak from your head?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when General Bobetko said that he didn't feel the meeting should discuss the items on the agenda, I simply took a map to the meeting, placed it in the room that we were in - I had a wooden pointer - stood before the map, and spent 35 minutes explaining the different positions and situation by pointing to the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, would you explain to us how this document had no registration number?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when this document -- I can't use the word "rejected," but when I was told that there was no need to have it processed further, that it should stay the way it was, so we didn't give it a registration number.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I see, thank you. Now, tell us, please, General, at the meeting did you see General Beneta?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, General Beneta was there, and there were four other people from the Municipal Staff of Capljina, led by Mr. Luburic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, as far as Bobetko was concerned, what did he see as being the most important thing at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, General Bobetko made two conclusions. The first conclusion was this: He asked to have in writing, first of all from me, and then 10 other commanders from the Municipal HVO Staff, that we should put down on paper and guarantee that the line established facing the Serbs had been secured and that no Serb forces would be able to break through the line and advance to the Neretva River. So that was the first assignment he gave me, the first guarantee he asked of us -- of myself and the other people there, and I did sign that. And he said, Right, I have this down on paper now with your signature, and I'm going to hold you to it. And, secondly, the second conclusion that he made was the following: He said, Think about having the remaining portion of the Croatian Army which I have to withdraw, think about how you're going to introduce the HVO army, and, secondly, set aside part of the forces and train them for further attack operations so that you are ready, if I'm successful and manage to route the Serb forces, that you could seize that opportunity. So be ready. And the third task was that there should be a firm link between positions in Herzegovina and positions of the Croatian Army along the borders of the -- the Croatian Army along the border towards Dubrovnik, to prevent anybody from infiltrating along that line. So those were the two main conclusions and assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is not my intention to discuss the document further. But if Your Honours have any questions, feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I have a question, because the situation in June 1992 is what I address it from, and then Bosnia and Herzegovina has been recognised by the international community and is a state. And you know better than anyone that a state has an army. And on that day, you organise a meeting, as it is indicated in the document, together with General Bobetko and some -- there are some commanders of the HVO from certain units, and political figureheads. And if I understood you correctly, you also said that Pasalic was there. And as the document states, you are setting forth the situation. And you take the floor. Your speech is structured. And on reading this document, I realise that the HVO has roughly a thousand men. You detail their strengths per locality. In Mostar, you say 3.500 to 3.700. That would total 10.000 in all. That would make up a division. And then you even add that there is the HOS that provided 80 to 100 men. And you then come up with a proposal - this is in paragraph 3 - based on the professional unit of Mr. Pusic, and you state that the army should become more professional and give the HVO soldiers a status. This is under item 4. You can read this document both ways. How is it, when a state has been created, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that you never say that there should be a professional army under the banner of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and so on, you don't say this at any point in time, why was this not mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, we're dealing with June 1992 here. The Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that point in time did not organise a single force in this territory here, except the independent battalion that was called "Mostar," and we paid all due attention to that. Now, in previous documents from the Ministry of Department [as interpreted] of Bosnia-Herzegovina, all recruits -- all conscripts should contact the municipal defence departments, be registered there, so that their units could be set up. Now, the Croatian Defence Council reacted to that and acted upon it. Now, at this point in time I did not have a single BH Army officer, except the independent battalion, as I said, not one single brigade or any kind of unit which was close to me and with whose commander I could reach an agreement. Therefore, all that existed was the Croatian Defence Council. There was part of the Croatian Army that helped liberate this area from the Army of Republika Srpska. And at that point in time, first of all, I did not know what was to the north of the army that was under the establishment of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I considered that since he sent this call-up for a general mobilisation, declared a situation of war, that is to say, the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that all people, myself and everybody else, all the other forces, were the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because otherwise he would have set up a force which he would have commanded. They did not do that. So most probably they counted upon the fact that in this area there were quite a number of troops that had already been established. And if you remember the documents from May onwards, President Izetbegovic was, in fact, establishing certain detachments and brigades, but they were all located in Central Bosnia, around Bihac, and nothing in this area. So as far as I was concerned, this meant to me that he had accepted the Croatian Defence Council fully as it was established in this territory here. On the other hand, as far as I remember, in this particular document I make no mention of Herceg-Bosna at all. I am -- I arrived in these parts two months prior to this, and I said straight away that items 2, 3, and 4 were my thoughts, comprised my thoughts, and they were not taken to the meeting. They were left behind for a more auspicious time, because I couldn't speak about professionalisation without a single document telling me what should be done and what legal foundations I would have. So that item was left for another time. And then I gave some thought to what had happened in Croatia and thought that it might be a good thing to apply something of that to Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I didn't mention Bosnia-Herzegovina at all, or Herceg-Bosna, for that matter. And, secondly, none of the municipal leaders came to attend the meeting. And I had been informed that they would be there, but they failed to arrive. So that was it. And in my opinion, as somebody who led part of the operation, all of us, to my mind, took part in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And, ultimately, the five of us were given the order of the Golden Lily in Sarajevo later on, regardless of the fact that my colleague, Halilovic, never came to congratulate me in the Presidency building that I was in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, a while ago, before we saw this document, I must say that I had listened very carefully to the demonstration you gave us on the question of the action conducted by the Croatian Army as regarded the Dubrovnik area, and you explained in detail what had been done and what you had done, and you said that you successfully managed to liberate some of the territories. I remembered this. And now we see this document, which is dated a few weeks later, and this doesn't seem to be saying quite the same thing. As you can see, if you look at item 1, you are saying that an offensive was launched in the south-east area by the HVO, with considerable assistance of the Croatian Army. When I listened to you a while ago, I had the feeling that it was the Croatian Army which had come because you were the only one there facing the Serbs, and now we discover in this document that there were HVO forces that took part in the fighting, with the assistance of the Croatian Army. The word "assistance" is in there. I had understood, from what you were saying before, that the Croatian Army, to protect its own interests, had stepped in to protect those interests. So I believe there is a contradiction here. Can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. It may be good to show the map again. The area in question is an area along the Croatian border, and you heard General Beneta's testimony. The Croatian Army was on a stretch of territory along the Croatian border. The depth of that territory was from 7 to 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we just show the map for Mr. Petkovic to show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to show you how it went. This direction [marks] is parallel to the Croatian border, and it is the direction of movement of the HV. Everything further north from this [marks] were directions of movement of the HVO, and thus we reached this line [marks]. That is the area along the border. Beneta was south of Stolac. Units of the HV were moving here, and from Stolac along the Bregava River and further north to Mostar, these were the directions of movement of the HVO. And here in the area of Mostar, they were also joined by this independent battalion of the BiH Army. And with your leave, once the HV and the HVO reached this line, the Croatian Army was in a position to move toward Dubrovnik more freely because its left flank is completely secured. That is, a part of the Serb forces was pushed back from the Croatian border, this border being protected by major forces, and the flanks of the HV are no longer open to operations of the VRS. And, thus, the HV got a manoeuvre capability to move forward to Dubrovnik. And that's what General Bobetko meant, that he needs a secure line as to have a safe flank, and it mustn't happen that the enemy move down the Neretva Valley and attack our forces from behind. And in July, in connection of Resolution -- whichever number it was, the Croatian Army started leaving this area and only stayed in the immediate vicinity of the border. On the 13th of July, General Bobetko ordered a pullout of the Croatian forces and the HVO forces were required to move in, because Bobetko wanted to move south toward Dubrovnik and didn't have other forces to count on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's give this an IC number. My colleague has several questions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The third marked version of document 4D02024 shall be given Exhibit IC01175. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have only one question, Mr. Petkovic, on this document, and we do not need the map for that. It refers to page 3 in the Croatian version, under number 3, "Profesionalizacija Vojske." In the first bullet point, the question is raised: "Which territory would such a professional army cover, the entire territory ..." And the word here is "prostor." It's not "territory" as in the first time when the word comes up. " ... the entire territory or just a part of it?" I would like you to explain to the Chamber what you meant by "entire territory."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I was drafting this, I meant exclusively the area of the 10 municipalities along the Neretva River, to put it that way; namely, the municipalities of Grude, Citluk, Siroki Brijeg, Mostar, Capljina, Stolac, Neum, Ravno. I may have left out one. I don't know. Anyway, my idea was that in this area there should be a professional unit, a regiment or a brigade, exclusively in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may have left out Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, I believe you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That completely answers my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A last question for you, Mr. Petkovic. At this meeting, you said that General Pasalic was there. Perhaps other Muslims were there also. I don't know; maybe, maybe not. But General Pasalic, who was listening to you talking about professional units, about a professional army, well, all that may be right for him. But you were a colonel of the Croatian Army. He could have thought, Why is he looking after our future army, because the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina exists. Maybe the Presidency of this republic should look after this, perhaps. Why is it that this Colonel from the Croatian Army is looking after this? Nobody made any comment in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, there were no comments to that effect. You're reading this off the paper, but it wasn't discussed at the meeting at all. I said that everything after item 2 was given up on. And there was no reason for Pasalic to foster misgivings against me, because his chief of Main Staff was from Serbia, so Bosnia was between the two. Halilovic, by the way, is not a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was born in Sandzak, which is in the then Socialist Republic of Serbia. But nobody would mind somebody coming to help, and that applies to Mr. Pasalic, too. And I believe that he was well informed about the structure of his battalion, brigade, and so on, how much of that he owed to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you take the floor before these elected officials in the municipality, were you aware of the political situation locally? Did you know anything about the ethnic breakdown? Did you have any idea of the census of 1992? Did you have any idea about the sensitive issue of Mostar? Did you know about this or didn't you? And you took the floor as a military who had conducted an action, and you are making proposals so that this military assignment be conducted by others?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had a view of the situation in these municipalities, so that I knew that in the municipality of Grude the population is almost inclusively [as interpreted] Croatian and that the Croatian party had won the elections. The same applies to Siroki Brijeg. When I say "elections," I mean the legal elections. In Citluk, there was an absolute Croatian majority. I also believe that the Croatian political party won the elections. Ljubuski, I wasn't sure of the relative shares in the population, but, anyway, the Croats were the majority and the Croatian political party had also won the elections. At Capljina, the situation was that the Croats were somewhat more numerous in the municipality, and I believe that in Capljina there was a coalition government of the HDZ and the SDA. I don't know what their respective shares were. At Neum, almost 100 per cent Croats. Again, Croats won the elections. Ravno, also 100 per cent or maybe 95 per cent of the population was Croatian. I'm not sure which villages are in the territory of the municipality. At Stolac, there was no local government at all, and earlier, as far as I knew at the time, Croats, Muslims, and Serbs were represented in government. Now only the Croats and Muslims only remained, but they were unable to establish government. In Mostar, the HDZ and the SDA participated in local government. I believe there was a share of Serbs. I don't know how many, though. But, basically, the HDZ and SDA were in power, and a decision was taken to entrust defence-related issues to the HVO. And the relative shares of the ethnicities in the former Mostar municipality, I think, was such that the Croats were slightly more numerous than the Muslims, and the Serbs were third, constituting half the share of either the Muslims or the Croats. I knew that and tried to consider all that, but it didn't -- it wasn't a problem for me because all the Muslims willing to fight were joining the HVO. The units were multi-ethnic. There was some mention of Herceg-Bosna, but nobody heeded that much at the time. What mattered was to be successful against the Serbs and then let them come to whatever agreement they can reach. At the time I am referring to in 1992, there were no obstacles in that part of Herzegovina, but, mind you, I didn't know about the situation in Central Bosnia because I never went there. And apart from that, I didn't have any authority to interfere with things in Central Bosnia. And it may be interesting for you to hear that Mr. Keza, who assisted me in drafting this item 1, said that it didn't really matter whether you say "Croatian," or what, because the people didn't mind much and they lived together in that area anyway. Later on, things may have changed, but while I was there for these two months, there was no reason for me to count people. So the information received from people was recorded by me, and I accepted what they had put down in writing and never opened a discussion about that. As for the term "Croatian," if anybody said "Croatian Mostar," of course, that could be understood to mean that no Muslims are there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you know that a document is read and then will be interpreted by the Judges, and the Prosecutor will also interpret all that. And I look at point 4, and you say that it's Keza who drafted this, and perhaps he was not very careful, and you took over from him. We have four points, 1, 2, 3, and 4. And point 4, it says that rules should be established in all municipalities. When we read that, we have the feeling that all municipalities in the area should be regulated by rules, but those rules should be for Croats, and we know that they are Muslims and Serbs as well. Is that a drafting mistake, or was that really the intent, or did it fail the attention of everyone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may intervene on a linguistic question. I think "rule" is not properly translated by "regle," but it is "dominance," it is the control. But perhaps the interpreters want to confirm or contradict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at your document. What is the word that was used? And as my colleagues said, perhaps there is an issue of translation from the original language. Could you perhaps read, in your own language, point 4 so that we have the translation immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reading item 4: "Establish Croatian rule or authority on municipalities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just wait a second. You can clarify this. But in your own language, it was translated into French and into English, and we have very good interpreters, it said: "Establish the Croatian powers in all municipalities." This was the translation that I got in French, so it goes beyond. There is a real power, isn't there, a real Croatian power? So my question remains the same. Is this a mistake in the way it was drafted by Keza? Did he not see the implications? Was that part of a definite intent or is there another explanation? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we look at item 4, it reads "in all municipalities ," but if we look at which particular municipalities this is referring to, then it doesn't make sense, because there are authorities in these municipalities. They were established in 1991, and since that time they've had the HVOs or whatever they were called. So this can be understood to mean that there are no authorities in Ravno, Neum, Capljina, Citluk, Ljubuski, et cetera. But there are authorities everywhere so that the only municipality with that authority is Stolac. This is not in line with the reality, because there were authorities in all municipalities apart from Stolac, and the authorities were elected in 1991. We saw how the process went of transforming those authorities into the HVO rule. So there were authorities, there was rule, so that this item 4 is out of sync with reality, because this can be understood to mean that in all 10 municipalities there are no authorities. In fact, there was only one such municipality, and that is Stolac. In all other municipalities, there were authorities established long before my arrival to those parts. I don't know when the elections were in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990. That's when authorities were established. The only municipality without legal authorities was Stolac. And you know that General Beneta said that a crisis staff was formed which had Muslim and Croat representatives, and that's when that municipality received authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, listening to you, one gets the impression that it was a matter of course that the authorities would be Croat, but that may be the issue, to establish Croat rule even where previously, as in Stolac, there was not a Croat rule and even a clear Muslim majority in the population. I think that was the point that the President was raising here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I'm talking using plural, and I said that at that moment the only place where there were no Croatian authorities was the municipality of Stolac. On the 26th of June, 1992, only Stolac municipality did not have any authority at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Let me immediately correct. The general didn't say did that there was no Croatian authorities. He said that there were no authorities at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't mention the word "Croatian." All those municipalities, save for Stolac, already had established authorities. Your Honour, those authorities had existed long before I arrived in the area. So why am I using plural? I really don't know. Why is this plural, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We understand what you're saying, but you are not a legal expert, nor a drafter of a document. But you say that point 4 was only dealing with Stolac. Very well. I have no reason not to believe you. But if this is the case, and this only applies to Stolac, why not say to establish in Stolac authorities with all political components of the municipality; namely, the SDA, the HDZ, and so on? Why not draft it that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's not up to me to think about that. At that moment, I was faced with the fact that the army had liberated Stolac and that there was nobody to hand over the power to, and that was that. The plural is used by mistake. There was nothing to change in Grude, Capljina, because the authorities were well established in all the other places. The only place in question is Stolac. And as I've already told you, this was taken off the typewriter. Nobody really looked at it twice. But let me say again that all the municipalities, except for Stolac, had legally-elected powers. And it was a well-established fact that in 75 per cent of -- in all those municipalities, Croats constituted more than 75 per cent of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you said there was a mistake, and it was only dealing with Stolac. So it's in the transcript. Ms. Alaburic, you have 10 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's be very clear and say: Was this document read at that meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, that document was not read. It could not have been read. It remained in Grude, and the meeting was held in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, you've told us that the persons who participated in the drafting of the document was Keza, Zadro, and yourself, and that the document was then read by Janko Bobetko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did anybody, except for the four of you, know about this document? Did anybody read it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, except for the lady who typed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now, General, could you please tell us, do you remember when Dubrovnik was liberated?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: In the first half of August 1992, that's when the blockade was lifted. It was always a free town, but what happened on that day, the blockade was lifted and it was linked up with the western part of Dubrovnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Please, let's look at P479. This is an invitation issued by Janko Bobetko and sent to people from Herceg-Bosna to a meeting in order to clarify certain circumstances regarding the military situation in the territory of Herzegovina. General, are you familiar with this document? Did you see it before?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it before, because I participated in the meeting and I had been given a task to deliver a keynote address and tackle certain issues. Items number 1 and 1.1 are my items, the ones that I discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the autumn of 1992, did Janko Bobetko stop being active in that part of the front-line?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one could say that at that moment General Janko Bobetko turned completely towards the liberation of the small remaining part of Croatia that was not liberated at the time, and then after that he left for Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, you also mentioned that you received a Golden Lily and that Halilovic never came to shake your hand and congratulate you. What were you talking about? Is that a decoration, the Golden Lily?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC
